In general, to determine the intervals of concavity of a particular function [MATH: f(x)], we need to solve

sections.readable_text: Determine the intervals on which the function [MATH: f(x) = x^3 -3x] is concave up.

sections.normalized_html:
A function [MATH: f(x)] is concave up on an interval [MATH: (a,b)] if [MATH: f''(x)> 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b).]

First, we calculate the second derivative of [MATH: f(x)= x^3 -3x \mathbin{:}] [MATH: f^{′}(x)|= 3x^{2} − 3; f^{″}(x)|= 6x]

Now, to find where the function is concave up, we solve the inequality [MATH: f''(x) > 0,] as follows:

[MATH: 6x|> 0; x|> 0]

Therefore, [MATH: f(x)] is concave up on [MATH: (0, \infty).]

sections.normalized_html: Find the intervals of concavity for the function [MATH: f(x) = 2 x^3 - x^4.]
sections.readable_text: Find the intervals of concavity for the function [MATH: f(x) = 2 x^3 - x^4.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we calculate the second derivative of [MATH: f(x),] as follows: [MATH: f(x)|= 2x^{3} − x^{4}; f^{′}(x)|= 6x^{2} − 4x^{3}; f^{″}(x)|= 12x − 12x^{2}]

To find where the function is concave up, we need to solve [MATH: f''(x) > 0\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 12x − 12x^{2}|> 0; 12x^{2} − 12x|< 0; x(x − 1)|< 0]

We can solve this inequality by considering the graph of [MATH: y=x(x-1).]

From the graph, we see that [MATH: x(x-1) < 0] when [MATH: 0 < x < 1.] So the graph is concave up on the interval [MATH: (0,1).]

The function [MATH: f(x)] is concave down when [MATH: f''(x) < 0.] By similar reasoning to before, this leads to the inequality [MATH: x(x-1) > 0,] which has the solution [MATH: (-\infty,0)] and [MATH: \left(1,\infty\right).]
